cards.front: How do C#, .NET, and ASP.NET Core fit together when building a website?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

C# is the language you write. .NET supplies the runtime that executes your application and libraries for common work. ASP.NET Core supplies web features such as routing requests and producing responses. The SDK provides development tools, including the compiler that checks and builds your code.

## A worked example

A browser requests /notes. ASP.NET Core matches that URL to your C# handler. The handler uses .NET libraries to do its work and returns a response. This path uses modern .NET, with .NET 10 as its baseline, rather than legacy System.Web tutorials.

## Picture it another way

C# is the language used in a recipe, .NET is the equipped kitchen, and ASP.NET Core is the service counter that accepts web orders.

## A common mistake

The .NET SDK and runtime serve different jobs. A computer running a framework-dependent app needs a compatible runtime; the machine building it needs the appropriate SDK.

## Try a small exercise

Which part matches an incoming HTTP request to your C# endpoint: the C# language itself or ASP.NET Core?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**ASP.NET Core** handles the web routing. C# expresses the endpoint logic, and .NET executes it. Separating these roles helps you choose the right documentation when debugging.

cards.front: Does var make a C# variable dynamically change its type?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

No. var asks the compiler to infer the variable's type from its initial value. Once inferred, that variable follows the normal type rules. An int inferred from a whole number does not become a string just because you later try to assign text.

## A worked example

```csharp
var attempts = 2;
attempts += 1;
Console.WriteLine(attempts); // 3
// attempts = "three"; // compile-time error
```

The compiler infers int on the first line. var saves typing the obvious type; it does not disable checking.

## Picture it another way

An unlabeled box can be identified from its contents. Once the label is inferred, the same storage rules still apply.

## A common mistake

Do not confuse var with dynamic. dynamic defers certain operations until runtime, which changes when mistakes are detected and is unnecessary for ordinary typed application code.

## Try a small exercise

After `var enabled = true;`, can ordinary C# code assign `enabled = "yes";`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** enabled has the inferred type bool, so assign true or false. Text states require a deliberately different type rather than an incompatible assignment.

cards.front: Why can dividing two C# integers discard the fractional part?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The operand types determine which operation runs. Dividing one int by another performs integer division, truncating toward zero. Use an appropriate fractional type when the result needs a fraction. decimal is useful when decimal precision and explicit rounding rules matter.

## A worked example

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(5 / 2);    // 2
Console.WriteLine(5m / 2m);  // 2.5 (culture affects display)
```

The m suffix creates decimal literals. Changing the destination type after integer division does not restore the fraction already discarded.

## Picture it another way

Splitting five indivisible tickets between two people gives two whole tickets each, with one left over. A divisible quantity needs a different representation.

## A common mistake

Do not assume `decimal result = 5 / 2;` produces 2.5. The right side performs integer division first, then converts the integer result to decimal.

## Try a small exercise

What value does `decimal average = 7 / 2;` store, and how could you preserve the fraction?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It stores **3**. Use decimal operands, such as `7m / 2m`, to obtain 3.5. Choose numeric types before arithmetic, not only when storing its result.

cards.front: What does the dollar sign before a C# string let you do?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An interpolated string allows expressions inside braces to contribute text. It is useful for readable labels and messages. The braces evaluate expressions; they do not automatically validate input or make text safe for every destination such as SQL or HTML.

## A worked example

```csharp
string name = "Ada";
int count = 3;
Console.WriteLine($"{name} has {count} notes.");
```

The output combines literal text with the current values of name and count. A normal string without the dollar sign does not evaluate those braces.

## Picture it another way

A mail-merge template fills labeled spaces with the recipient's information. The template remains readable while values vary.

## A common mistake

Do not assume interpolating a value into arbitrary SQL text is parameterization. Use a database API designed to bind parameters; API-specific interpolated handlers have their own contracts.

## Try a small exercise

What does `Console.WriteLine("Total: {2 + 3}");` print without a dollar sign?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It prints **Total: {2 + 3}** literally. `$"Total: {2 + 3}"` instead evaluates the expression and produces Total: 5.

cards.front: What do int? and string? communicate when you read C# code?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

int? is a nullable value type that can contain an integer or null. With nullable reference types enabled, string? tells the compiler that a string reference may be null. The reference-type annotation helps checking but does not insert runtime validation for external data.

## A worked example

```csharp
int? age = null;
string? nickname = null;
Console.WriteLine(age ?? 0);
Console.WriteLine(nickname?.Length ?? 0);
```

?? supplies a fallback for null. ?. skips member access when the receiver is null. Both printed values are zero in this example.

## Picture it another way

An optional form field needs a way to distinguish no answer from a real answer such as zero. The type communicates that possibility.

## A common mistake

The null-forgiving operator ! suppresses warnings; it does not create a missing object. Validate external input rather than silencing the evidence that it may be absent.

## Try a small exercise

Does writing `user!.Name` prevent a runtime failure if user actually is null?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The exclamation mark changes compiler analysis, not the value. Check for null or establish a valid user before accessing Name.

cards.front: How is a C# if condition different from JavaScript truthiness?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Ordinary C# if conditions require a boolean expression. Integers and strings do not automatically become true or false as they do in JavaScript conditions. Write the actual condition, such as a positive count or a nonempty name, so the intended rule is explicit.

## A worked example

```csharp
int count = 2;
if (count > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Items available");
}
```

count > 0 evaluates to bool. Replacing it with count alone would not be valid for an int condition.

## Picture it another way

A gate asks a specific yes-or-no question instead of guessing what a supplied number should mean.

## A common mistake

A non-null string can still be empty or whitespace. Use the condition your form actually requires, such as !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name).

## Try a small exercise

Why is `if (quantity)` invalid when quantity is an ordinary C# int?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An int is not implicitly a bool in that condition. Write the intended question, such as `quantity > 0`, rather than relying on JavaScript-style truthiness.

cards.front: What information does a C# method signature provide to its caller?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It names the operation, specifies the input parameters, and declares the return type. A non-void return gives the caller a result to use. Parameter names explain the roles of the values; parameter types constrain which values can be supplied.

## A worked example

```csharp
int Add(int left, int right)
{
    return left + right;
}
Console.WriteLine(Add(2, 4)); // 6
```

This local function accepts two integers and returns an integer. The caller receives the result rather than merely observing a console message inside the function.

## Picture it another way

A service menu describes what you order and what you receive. The method body explains how the service performs the work.

## A common mistake

Console.WriteLine is not a replacement for return when another method needs the result. Printing is an output side effect, while return passes data back to the caller.

## Try a small exercise

If a method is declared `bool IsAvailable(int stock)`, what kind of value should its normal return paths provide?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A **bool**, such as the result of `stock > 0`. The int is the input type; bool is the output type promised to callers.

cards.front: Why is int.TryParse useful for text entered in a web form?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

TryParse reports success as a boolean and supplies the parsed value through an out parameter. Invalid user input is an expected possibility, so it can take a normal validation path. Parsing establishes a number; a separate check establishes whether the number is acceptable for your feature.

## A worked example

```csharp
string input = "12";
if (int.TryParse(input, out int quantity) && quantity > 0)
{
    Console.WriteLine(quantity); // 12
}
```

The second check runs only if parsing succeeds. A parsed negative number still fails the business rule.

## Picture it another way

First check whether a ticket can be read, then check whether it is valid for this trip. Readability and eligibility are different checks.

## A common mistake

Do not use the output value as if parsing succeeded when TryParse returned false. Also define culture and accepted formatting when parsing dates or decimal user input.

## Try a small exercise

If int.TryParse successfully parses "-3", does that prove the value is a valid order quantity?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Parsing proves it is representable as an int. Apply a separate rule such as quantity > 0 and any upper limit required by the application.

cards.front: How is a C# class different from an object created from it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A class describes fields, properties, and behavior. An object is a particular instance with its own state. Calling new creates an instance. Two notes can use the same class while carrying different titles; they do not become one note just because their type matches.

## A worked example

```csharp
var first = new Note { Title = "Routing" };
var second = new Note { Title = "LINQ" };
Console.WriteLine(first.Title); // Routing
class Note
{
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
}
```

The declarations use top-level program syntax, with the class after the executable statements.

## Picture it another way

A blank form template resembles a class. Each filled-in form is a separate instance with its own information.

## A common mistake

Assigning an existing class instance to another variable does not create another instance. Both variables then refer to the same object unless you explicitly create or copy one.

## Try a small exercise

After `var b = a;` where a refers to a Note object, does changing b.Title usually change the title seen through a?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Yes.** a and b refer to the same class instance. A second variable is not a deep copy of the note.

cards.front: What do get and set describe in a C# property?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

get describes reading the property and set describes assigning it. Auto-properties provide ordinary storage with concise syntax. Restricting the setter can keep callers from bypassing a rule, while methods expose meaningful changes to the object.

## A worked example

```csharp
var counter = new Counter();
counter.Increment();
Console.WriteLine(counter.Value); // 1
class Counter
{
    public int Value { get; private set; }
    public void Increment() => Value++;
}
```

Outside code can read Value but changes it through Increment rather than directly assigning arbitrary values.

## Picture it another way

A display window lets customers see a balance; authorized operations behind the counter decide how the balance changes.

## A common mistake

A private setter is an in-process design rule, not an API permission check. Server endpoints still need authorization and input validation.

## Try a small exercise

Can unrelated outside code assign Value on a property declared `public int Value { get; private set; }`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Outside callers can read it but cannot use its private setter. The containing type decides how its state may change through its accessible operations.

cards.front: Why put required dependencies or values in a C# constructor?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A constructor runs when an instance is created. Requiring necessary inputs there makes it harder to create an object that cannot perform its job. It can reject invalid initial values or accept the services the object will need.

## A worked example

```csharp
var note = new Note("Queues");
Console.WriteLine(note.Title);
class Note
{
    public string Title { get; }
    public Note(string title) => Title = title;
}
```

This constructor requires a title argument. A real domain rule may also reject blank titles; the signature alone does not enforce that rule.

## Picture it another way

A rental desk asks for the essential details before issuing a rental agreement, rather than creating a half-filled agreement for later repair.

## A common mistake

Avoid doing slow network work in constructors. Object creation is usually easier to reason about when asynchronous loading is an explicit operation.

## Try a small exercise

Does a constructor parameter typed string automatically reject empty text?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Empty text is still a string. Add explicit validation where nonempty content is required; type checking and domain rules solve different parts of the problem.

cards.front: How can a C# interface help a service work with different implementations?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An interface describes the members a caller can rely on. A class can implement that contract, and the caller can use the interface without knowing every implementation detail. This is useful at boundaries such as clocks, storage, or external message sending.

## A worked example

```csharp
IGreeting greeting = new FriendlyGreeting();
Console.WriteLine(greeting.Text());
interface IGreeting { string Text(); }
class FriendlyGreeting : IGreeting
{
    public string Text() => "Hello";
}
```

The caller knows Text is available. It does not need to know how FriendlyGreeting constructs the message.

## Picture it another way

An electrical socket defines a connection that many appliances can implement. The shared connection is more stable than each appliance's internal mechanism.

## A common mistake

Do not add an interface to every tiny class automatically. Introduce a useful boundary or contract, rather than extra types that merely repeat implementation names.

## Try a small exercise

Why might an email service accept an IMessageSender instead of directly constructing a specific provider client?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It can rely on a defined sending contract while configuration supplies the implementation. Tests can use a controlled sender and production can use the appropriate provider adapter.

Composition is not a reason to scatter a tiny feature across dozens of classes. Keep boundaries aligned with clear responsibilities and real variation.

cards.front: Why are C# records useful for small request or response data types?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Records provide concise data declarations and generated value-based equality over their members. They can make an API data shape easy to read. A record does not automatically validate data, deeply freeze nested objects, or replace a thoughtful boundary between storage and public responses.

## A worked example

```csharp
var a = new NoteDto(7, "LINQ");
var b = new NoteDto(7, "LINQ");
Console.WriteLine(a == b); // True
record NoteDto(int Id, string Title);
```

For these simple value members, the generated equality compares their contents. Ordinary class equality has different defaults.

## Picture it another way

Two printed labels can represent the same information even though they are different sheets of paper. A data record makes that comparison convenient.

## A common mistake

A record containing a mutable list is not deeply immutable. The list may still change, and the member's own equality behavior affects record equality.

## Try a small exercise

Does putting a List<string> inside a C# record automatically prevent callers from adding items to that list?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Record syntax does not recursively freeze referenced objects. Choose an appropriate representation and ownership policy when data must remain unchanged.

cards.front: Why use a create-request DTO instead of accepting an entire database entity from a client?
cards.back:

## Plain English

A data transfer object defines the fields the client is allowed to supply. A database entity may also contain ownership, timestamps, or internal flags that the client must not control. Map accepted input deliberately and derive authoritative fields on the server.

A DTO does not itself provide authorization or enforce every business rule. Validate accepted fields and check the caller's rights at the appropriate server boundary.

Should a note-creation DTO normally let the browser choose the authoritative owner ID?

**No.** Derive ownership from the authenticated context or an explicitly authorized delegation rule. A client-supplied owner ID is data to verify, not proof of permission.

cards.front: Why is catching every C# exception and returning success misleading?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An exception signals that an operation did not complete normally. Handle it where you can recover, translate it into a meaningful outcome, or record useful diagnostic context. Claiming success after a failed save causes the caller to believe data exists when it may not.

## A worked example

If saving a note fails, an endpoint should return an appropriate failure response while a central handler logs useful context. Inside a catch block, `throw;` rethrows the current exception while preserving its stack information better than `throw ex;`.

## Picture it another way

A delivery company should report a failed delivery instead of printing a delivered receipt. The caller needs the real outcome to decide what to do next.

## A common mistake

Do not expose raw exception details, connection strings, or stack traces in production responses. Keep diagnostics in appropriate logs and use safe error messages for callers.

## Try a small exercise

Inside a catch block, which rethrow preserves the original exception path: `throw;` or `throw ex;`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Use **throw;** to rethrow the current exception without resetting the original throw location. Add context through suitable logging or intentional exception wrapping when needed.

cards.front: What does List<Note> tell you about a C# collection?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It is a list whose elements have the Note type. Lists preserve order and provide indexed access, while their size can change. The generic element type lets the compiler check additions and gives readers a clear picture of the collection's contents.

## A worked example

```csharp
var titles = new List<string> { "HTTP", "LINQ" };
titles.Add("EF Core");
Console.WriteLine(titles[0]); // HTTP
Console.WriteLine(titles.Count); // 3
```

Indexes start at zero. Count is the number of items, so the final valid index is Count - 1 when the list is nonempty.

## Picture it another way

A numbered row of storage slots keeps order while allowing more slots to be appended. The labels specify what kind of item belongs there.

## A common mistake

Do not access position zero before establishing that the list has an item. An empty list is a valid collection but has no valid element index.

## Try a small exercise

For a C# list with Count equal to 3, is index 3 a valid element position?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The valid positions are 0, 1, and 2. Count describes how many elements exist, not the index of the last one.

cards.front: When is a C# Dictionary a useful alternative to scanning a list?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A dictionary maps keys to values and supports efficient lookup by key in typical use. It fits tasks such as finding a count by category. Keys are unique within the dictionary, while different keys may map to equal values.

## A worked example

```csharp
var counts = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["api"] = 3 };
if (counts.TryGetValue("api", out int count))
{
    Console.WriteLine(count); // 3
}
```

TryGetValue separates the found case from a missing key. Indexer reads of missing keys throw instead.

## Picture it another way

A labeled cabinet lets you go directly to a folder name instead of inspecting every folder in a pile.

## A common mistake

A normal Dictionary is not a general solution for simultaneous mutation from multiple threads. Choose suitable synchronization or a concurrent collection when state is actually shared.

## Try a small exercise

Why use TryGetValue when a dictionary key may legitimately be absent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It reports absence through a boolean so you can take a normal fallback path. This avoids treating an expected missing key as a successful lookup or relying on an exception for that case.

cards.front: In a LINQ Where call, what should the supplied lambda return?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Where uses a predicate: a function that returns true to keep an item and false to exclude it. It filters the sequence without transforming each kept value. Reading the condition aloud often makes the business rule easier to verify.

## A worked example

```csharp
int[] scores = { 2, 7, 4 };
var passing = scores.Where(score => score >= 4);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", passing)); // 7,4
```

The lambda asks a yes-or-no question for each score. The original array is not modified.

## Picture it another way

A gate admits only tickets that satisfy a rule. Admitted tickets remain the same tickets; the gate does not rewrite them.

## A common mistake

Do not confuse Where with Select. Filtering decides which items remain, while projection decides what output value each item produces.

## Try a small exercise

For `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, what does a LINQ filter with `n => n % 2 == 0` keep?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**2 and 4.** The remainder is zero for even numbers. The predicate keeps those values and excludes the odd ones.

cards.front: What does Select change when you build a LINQ pipeline?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Select projects each input item into an output value. It can extract a field, calculate a value, or build a response DTO. For database-backed queries, a suitable projection can also reduce the columns returned from the database.

## A worked example

```csharp
string[] titles = { "api", "linq" };
var labels = titles.Select(title => title.ToUpperInvariant());
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", labels)); // API,LINQ
```

Every title contributes one transformed value. This example uses invariant casing for a predictable demonstration.

## Picture it another way

A mailing-label machine takes each customer record and prints only the fields needed on the envelope.

## A common mistake

A Select expression over IQueryable must be supported by the database provider or handled according to EF Core's translation rules. Arbitrary C# methods are not automatically SQL.

## Try a small exercise

If an API response needs only a note ID and title, why project those fields before materializing an EF Core query?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The provider can often fetch only the required data. Loading entire entities first may transfer and track unnecessary fields, increasing work before the response is created.

cards.front: How do First and FirstOrDefault differ in LINQ when nothing matches?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

First throws when the sequence has no matching item. FirstOrDefault returns the element type's default instead. For a reference type that is usually null; for an int it is zero. Choose the method and absence policy deliberately rather than treating a default as proof of a match.

## A worked example

```csharp
string[] names = { "Ada", "Lin" };
string? found = names.FirstOrDefault(n => n == "Jo");
Console.WriteLine(found ?? "Not found");
```

No name matches, so the fallback is displayed. A database lookup needs an equivalent explicit missing-resource outcome.

## Picture it another way

A search desk can either require a matching record or return a marked no-result slip. Those policies communicate different expectations.

## A common mistake

FirstOrDefault does not assert uniqueness. If multiple results indicate corrupt or ambiguous data, consider a uniqueness constraint and an appropriate Single/SingleOrDefault policy.

## Try a small exercise

Why can zero from FirstOrDefault over integers be ambiguous?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Zero can be either a real matching value or the default for an empty result. Represent absence explicitly when the caller needs to distinguish those cases.

cards.front: Why can changing a list after declaring a LINQ query affect its later results?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Many LINQ operators use deferred execution: declaring the query describes work, while enumeration performs it. If the underlying data changes before enumeration, the query can observe those changes. Materializing into a list captures results at that moment, subject to ordinary reference-copy behavior.

## A worked example

```csharp
var numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2 };
var query = numbers.Where(n => n > 1);
numbers.Add(3);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", query)); // 2,3
```

The filtering happens when string.Join enumerates query, after 3 was added.

## Picture it another way

Writing a shopping plan does not buy the items immediately. The available stock when you execute the plan can differ from when you wrote it.

## A common mistake

Enumerating a database query twice can execute two database operations. Materialize once when you intentionally need to reuse the same result set.

## Try a small exercise

Does assigning `var query = items.Where(test);` normally create a frozen copy of the filtered items?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It usually creates a deferred sequence. Use a deliberate materialization step such as ToList when you need the results collected now.

For an EF Core DbSet, apply an appropriate Where and Select before ToListAsync. The provider can translate those operations and fetch a focused result. Calling ToList first loads the earlier query's results before later in-memory filtering.

Sending a librarian a search request differs from asking for every book and searching your own pile. Where the work happens changes the cost.

Why can calling ToList before Where be expensive on a large EF Core table?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It materializes the broader dataset first. The subsequent filter works in application memory, so rows that could have been excluded by SQL may already have been transferred.

cards.back:

## Plain English

Several records can have equal values in the primary sort field. A unique tie-breaker makes their relative order defined, which helps keep pages consistent. Use ThenBy to add a secondary order; a new OrderBy starts a new primary ordering.

## A worked example

An EF Core query can order by CreatedAt and then Id before applying a bounded Take. Cursor pagination must use the same ordering fields when identifying where the next page starts. Deterministic order alone does not prevent every change caused by concurrent inserts.

## Picture it another way

Two people can share a surname. Adding a unique ticket number gives the clerk a dependable way to order them.

## A common mistake

Do not rely on a database's incidental physical row order. Results without a specified ORDER BY have no guaranteed presentation sequence.

## Try a small exercise

To sort by team and then name in LINQ, should the second operation normally be OrderBy or ThenBy?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**ThenBy.** It adds a secondary ordering within equal teams. Another OrderBy establishes a new primary order instead of expressing that intended hierarchy.

cards.front: What does await do when a C# asynchronous operation has not finished yet?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

await lets the method pause its progress until the operation finishes, while returning control to its caller. The waiting thread does not need to remain blocked. After completion, execution continues with the result or an exception. async does not automatically put all work on another thread.

## A worked example

```csharp
async Task<int> ReadLater()
{
    await Task.Delay(10);
    return 7;
}
int value = await ReadLater();
Console.WriteLine(value); // 7
```

The delay stands in for work that completes later. Task<int> represents the eventual integer result.

## Picture it another way

Leave an order ticket and return when the kitchen signals readiness instead of occupying the counter while nothing can be collected.

## A common mistake

CPU-heavy work before the first incomplete await still runs synchronously on the calling thread. Using the async keyword alone does not make a slow calculation cheap.

## Try a small exercise

Does marking a C# method async guarantee that its expensive calculation runs on a background thread?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** async enables await-based control flow. CPU work still needs an appropriate execution strategy; it does not move to another thread merely because the method is async.

cards.front: Why avoid Task.Result and Wait in an ASP.NET Core request path?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

They block the calling thread while waiting. Under load, many blocked request threads can reduce capacity and contribute to thread-pool starvation. Prefer awaiting asynchronous I/O through the call chain. Deadlock risks depend on the synchronization context, so blocking is not automatically a deadlock in every application.

## A worked example

In an async endpoint, use `await service.LoadAsync(cancellationToken)` and return a Task-based result. Calling `.Result` on that task turns the wait into a blocked thread without making the remote work finish sooner.

## Picture it another way

Every waiter standing motionless at the kitchen door leaves fewer waiters available to serve other tables. Waiting efficiently matters when many requests overlap.

## A common mistake

Wrapping every blocking call in Task.Run does not remove its resource cost. Use genuinely asynchronous APIs for I/O where available and bound expensive background work.

## Try a small exercise

A server has hundreds of requests blocked on databaseTask.Result. Does adding async to the method declaration alone fix the blocking?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Replace the blocking wait with await and propagate the asynchronous return through callers. The keyword alone does not change what Result does.

cards.front: When can Task.WhenAll improve an async C# workflow?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

If operations are independent and safe to overlap, start them before awaiting their combined completion. WhenAll waits for all supplied tasks. It does not impose a concurrency limit, make shared objects thread-safe, or guarantee that every remote dependency benefits from extra parallel requests.

## A worked example

```csharp
Task<int> First() => Task.FromResult(2);
Task<int> Second() => Task.FromResult(5);
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(First(), Second());
Console.WriteLine(results.Sum()); // 7
```

The result array follows the input task order. Real I/O tasks may complete in a different order.

## Picture it another way

You can order two independent dishes together, but the kitchen still has limited capacity and shared equipment.

## A common mistake

Do not run simultaneous EF Core operations on one DbContext through WhenAll. That context is not thread-safe; use sequential awaits or appropriate separate contexts for independent work.

## Try a small exercise

Does Task.WhenAll automatically limit a list of 10,000 outbound requests to a small safe concurrency level?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It waits for the supplied tasks. Use explicit bounded concurrency and an appropriate request budget when starting large amounts of work.

cards.front: How can a CancellationToken help an ASP.NET Core endpoint stop unnecessary work?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A token communicates that work is no longer wanted, such as when a request is aborted. Pass it to operations that support cancellation and observe it in longer loops. Cancellation is cooperative: it requests a stop, not a guaranteed rollback of every effect already completed.

## A worked example

A Minimal API can accept a CancellationToken parameter, which represents request cancellation. Pass it to EF Core ToListAsync or HttpClient calls. Otherwise those operations may continue using resources after the original caller disconnects.

## Picture it another way

A customer cancels an order, and the counter relays that message to the kitchen. The message helps only if the kitchen actually checks it.

## A common mistake

Do not report every OperationCanceledException as an unexpected server crash. Distinguish expected request cancellation while still understanding whether important side effects already happened.

## Try a small exercise

Does canceling a token guarantee that an already committed database write is undone?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Cancellation affects cooperative work that observes it. A completed commit remains a completed effect; transactional and retry behavior need their own explicit design.

cards.front: Why should ordinary asynchronous C# service methods return Task rather than async void?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A Task lets callers await completion and observe failure. async void provides no such task, making sequencing and exception handling much harder. It is mainly needed for certain event-handler signatures, not ordinary request handlers or business-service methods.

## A worked example

Define `Task SaveNoteAsync(...)` so the endpoint can await it before returning success. If the method were async void, the endpoint could finish its response while the save was still running or later failed.

## Picture it another way

A claim ticket lets you check when a job finishes. Handing off work without any completion signal leaves the caller guessing.

## A common mistake

Ignoring a returned Task can cause similar problems even when the signature is correct. Decide who owns and observes the operation through completion.

## Try a small exercise

Why can an endpoint that calls an async void save method return 200 too early?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It has no returned Task to await, so it cannot reliably wait for the save. Return and await Task so the response can reflect completion or an appropriate failure.

cards.front: What does using do for a disposable C# resource?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A using statement or declaration ensures disposal when control leaves its scope, including exceptional exits. This helps release resources such as streams. await using supports resources with asynchronous disposal. The owner of a resource normally decides when its lifetime ends.

## A worked example

```csharp
using var stream = new MemoryStream(new byte[] { 1, 2 });
Console.WriteLine(stream.ReadByte()); // 1
```

The stream is disposed when this scope ends. A resource supplied by dependency injection may instead be owned and disposed by the container.

## Picture it another way

Borrow equipment for a defined shift and return it at the end, even if the job ends unexpectedly.

## A common mistake

Do not return a stream for later use after disposing it in the current method. Coordinate its ownership with the component that must finish reading it.

## Try a small exercise

If a method returns a stream but its using scope closes before the caller reads it, what can go wrong?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The caller receives an already disposed resource. Keep the stream alive for its intended consumer or return fully materialized data when that is the appropriate contract.

cards.front: Why is IHttpClientFactory useful in an ASP.NET Core service?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The factory creates configured HttpClient instances while managing underlying handler lifetimes. Named or typed clients organize settings for particular APIs. This helps avoid ad hoc per-request handler creation and centralizes timeouts, base addresses, and message handlers.

## A worked example

Register a named client with AddHttpClient before building the app. A service requests that client from IHttpClientFactory and awaits its calls, passing cancellation. Long-lived HttpClient instances can also be valid with a correctly configured connection lifetime.

## Picture it another way

A managed transport desk maintains reusable vehicles and provides the right settings for each route. Every passenger need not build a new vehicle.

Do not assume factory usage makes every retry safe. Retried writes may duplicate effects, and the client still needs appropriate limits and response handling.

## Try a small exercise

Does IHttpClientFactory mean your application no longer needs to check HTTP error statuses?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It manages client configuration and handler lifetimes. Your service still needs to interpret the response, handle failure, and respect cancellation and deadlines.

cards.front: Why is starting an unobserved Task from a web request a fragile way to send important email?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The request can end, its scoped services can be disposed, and the process can stop before the task completes. Important longer work needs a defined owner, failure handling, and often a durable queue. A hosted service manages lifetime but does not by itself make an in-memory queue durable.

## A worked example

An endpoint records a durable email job and returns an accepted status. A worker processes it with its own service scope, records the result, and handles retries. Database changes and job publication may need an outbox to avoid a crash between separate writes.

## Picture it another way

A shop gives a repair job to a tracked work queue instead of asking a departing visitor to carry the task in their pocket.

## A common mistake

Do not capture a request-scoped DbContext for work that outlives the request. Create an appropriate worker scope or context when processing the job.

## Try a small exercise

Does BackgroundService alone guarantee that a queued job survives a server restart?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It coordinates hosted work while the process runs. Persistence and recovery require an appropriate durable store or message system and explicit processing rules.

cards.front: What do CreateBuilder, Build, MapGet, and Run do in a small ASP.NET Core app?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

CreateBuilder prepares configuration and service registration. Build creates the web application. MapGet associates a GET route with a handler. Run starts the host so it can accept requests. Services are normally registered on the builder before Build.

## A worked example

In Program.cs of a .NET 10 web project:

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapGet("/hello", () => "Hello from C#");
app.Run();
```

A GET to /hello invokes the lambda and receives the text response. Declaring the route is separate from receiving a request.

## Picture it another way

Prepare a service desk, assign a station to a request type, then open the doors. Customers cannot arrive until the host is running.

## A common mistake

Do not put service registrations after Build and expect the built provider to gain them. Separate setup from the running request pipeline.

## Try a small exercise

In a Minimal API, does writing app.MapGet call the handler immediately for a real HTTP request?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It registers how matching requests will be handled. The handler runs later when the running application receives a suitable request.

Endpoint registration excerpt, after app is built:

A numbered counter window directs a request to the right slot. The slot number does not prove there is a valid item waiting inside.

cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It provides a typed shape for deserializing accepted fields. Successful binding means the data could be represented in that shape, not that every business rule passed. Required content, maximum lengths, and permissions still need the appropriate validation and authorization.

## A worked example

Endpoint excerpt; declare the record after top-level statements:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/notes", (CreateNote request) =>
    Results.Ok(new { request.Title }));
// Type declaration goes after app.Run() in Program.cs:
record CreateNote(string Title);
```

This only echoes input to demonstrate binding. It does not persist a note.

## Picture it another way

A form gives each answer a named box. Filling those boxes is separate from approving whether the answers are acceptable.

## A common mistake

cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

cards.front: What does dependency injection do for an ASP.NET Core handler?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The application registers how required services are created. A handler or class declares its dependencies, and the container supplies them according to those registrations and lifetimes. This separates the work a feature performs from the details of constructing every collaborator.

## A worked example

Register `builder.Services.AddScoped<NoteService>()` before Build. A Minimal API handler can then declare a NoteService parameter, which the framework resolves from services. NoteService must be a real application type with dependencies the container can also resolve.

## Picture it another way

A workshop supplies tools to a worker at the start of a job. The worker can focus on the task instead of manufacturing every tool.

Do not call BuildServiceProvider ad hoc during normal registration to get another provider. That can create duplicate singleton instances and confusing ownership.

## Try a small exercise

If a handler requests a service whose constructor needs an unregistered dependency, what should you investigate?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Check the registration chain and constructors. The container must be able to supply each required dependency with a suitable lifetime; requesting a service does not invent its implementation.

cards.front: How do transient, scoped, and singleton services differ in a typical ASP.NET Core request app?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Transient creates a new instance per resolution. Scoped reuses an instance within a scope, usually an HTTP request. Singleton reuses one instance from the application's container. The choice affects sharing, cleanup, and whether state can accidentally leak between requests.

## A worked example

A request-specific unit of work often fits a scoped lifetime. A stateless utility may fit transient. A shared singleton must be designed for concurrent use and must not store one caller's private request data as if it belonged to everyone.

## Picture it another way

One tool per handoff, one toolkit per job, and one shared machine for the whole workshop represent three different sharing policies.

Scoped does not always mean one browser visit. For example, interactive Blazor server scopes have a different lifetime from ordinary HTTP request scopes.

Why is a mutable CurrentUser field on a singleton service dangerous in a web app?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Different requests can share that same instance. One user's value may overwrite another's, creating races or data leakage. Keep request-specific identity in the appropriate request context or scope.

cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The singleton lives longer than a request scope. Capturing the scoped dependency effectively extends its use beyond its intended lifetime and can share non-thread-safe state across requests. Lifetime validation can catch this mismatch; disabling it does not repair the design.

A hosted worker is long-lived. For one job, it can create a service scope, resolve the scoped service there, await the work, and dispose the scope. Alternatively, use an appropriate context factory for the unit of work.

Keeping a visitor's temporary desk key forever does not make it a valid building-wide key. The owner and lifetime still matter.

Do not resolve a scoped service once at startup and reuse it for every background job. Create a valid lifetime boundary for each unit of work.

cards.front: What does calling next mean inside ASP.NET Core middleware?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Middleware can do work before passing control to the next component, and after that component returns. It can also end the request early. Registration order determines how these pieces wrap one another, which affects errors, authentication, headers, and other behavior.

## A worked example

Pipeline excerpt:

```csharp
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-App"] = "Recall";
    await next(context);
});
```

This adds a demonstration header before later middleware or the endpoint runs. It does not replace any required security middleware.

## Picture it another way

A visitor passes through reception before reaching a meeting room, then returns through reception afterward. Each station can act on the way in or out.

## A common mistake

Response headers may be read-only after the body starts. Set them at a suitable earlier point or use the correct response-start callback for the requirement.

## Try a small exercise

If middleware never calls next and writes a response, does the endpoint necessarily run?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The middleware can short-circuit the pipeline. This is intentional for some cases, but accidental omission can prevent all downstream handling.

cards.front: What job does an EF Core DbContext perform during a typical request?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It coordinates queries, tracked entities, and saving changes for a unit of work. It is designed for a short, appropriate lifetime and is not thread-safe. A request-scoped context is common for HTTP APIs, while other application models may need a context factory or explicit scope.

## A worked example

An update handler loads a note through its context, changes an allowed field, awaits SaveChangesAsync, and finishes. The context tracks the changes during that unit of work; it is not a shared application-wide cache of all users' entities.

## Picture it another way

A clerk opens a worksheet for one transaction, records its edits, submits them, and closes the worksheet. Sharing one worksheet across every customer would mix unrelated work.

## A common mistake

Do not start a second operation on the same context before awaiting the first. Using async does not make DbContext safe for simultaneous calls.

## Try a small exercise

Can two queries safely run in parallel through the same DbContext simply because both use ToListAsync?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The context does not support concurrent operations. Await sequentially or use appropriately independent contexts when parallel work is justified.

cards.front: What is an EF Core entity, and why does its key matter?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An entity is a type included in the persistence model. Its key identifies a record so the context and database can distinguish updates and relationships. Not every response object needs to be an entity; public DTOs can describe a narrower external contract.

## A worked example

An entity declaration excerpt:

```csharp
public class Note
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Title { get; set; } = "";
}
```

EF Core conventions commonly recognize Id as a key when this type is included in the model. Provider and model configuration determine storage behavior.

## Picture it another way

A library inventory number distinguishes two copies with the same title. The title alone is not a dependable record identity.

## A common mistake

Do not assume every C# property rule automatically becomes an appropriate database constraint. Review the actual model and generated schema, including lengths, nullability, and unique rules.

Why is a note's title usually a poor replacement for a stable primary key?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Titles can change or repeat. A stable key lets references and updates identify the same record independently of its current display text.

cards.front: When is AsNoTracking useful in an EF Core query?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It avoids ordinary change tracking for returned entities, which can reduce work for read-only queries. Tracking is useful when you intend to modify a loaded entity and let SaveChanges detect those edits. Choose based on the operation rather than applying one policy blindly.

## A worked example

Read-only query excerpt with an existing context and token:

```csharp
var notes = await db.Notes.AsNoTracking()
    .Where(n => n.Id > 0)
    .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
```

The example assumes Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore is imported. A public endpoint should also filter by the caller's access rules.

## Picture it another way

Reading a reference copy does not require opening an editing worksheet for every line. Tracking is useful when changes are part of the intended job.

Editing an untracked object and calling SaveChanges does not automatically attach that object. Use a deliberate update strategy and avoid marking arbitrary client-supplied fields as modified.

cards.front: Why must an EF Core create operation call SaveChangesAsync after Add?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Add tells the context to track an entity as something to insert. SaveChangesAsync sends the pending changes to the database. Until the save completes successfully, the application should not claim that the new row is durably stored.

## A worked example

Persistence excerpt:

```csharp
var note = new Note { Title = "Transactions" };
db.Notes.Add(note);
await db.SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken);
```

The context, entity model, and provider are configured elsewhere. The await ensures subsequent code sees the save outcome rather than racing ahead.

## Picture it another way

Putting a form in the outgoing tray is not the same as the records office accepting it. The save is the submission step.

## A common mistake

SaveChanges can fail because of constraints, connectivity, or concurrent changes. Handle the failure at the appropriate boundary instead of returning a successful creation receipt anyway.

## Try a small exercise

Does db.Notes.Add(note) by itself guarantee that another database connection can retrieve the new note?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It queues a tracked insertion in the context. The change must be saved successfully, and surrounding transaction boundaries also affect when other connections can observe it.

cards.front: What is the purpose of an EF Core database migration?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A migration records a model-related schema change so databases can be moved between defined versions. Review the generated operations and deploy them intentionally. Updating a C# class alone does not necessarily update the deployed database schema.

## A worked example

After adding a required title-length rule, generate a migration and inspect what it changes. Existing data may need cleanup or a backfill before a new constraint can be enforced. Apply the migration through the project's chosen deployment process.

## Picture it another way

Changing a building plan does not move the walls. A migration is the planned construction work that brings the real building into line with the plan.

## A common mistake

Do not casually apply destructive migrations to production or assume every application instance should race to migrate the database at startup. Plan ownership, compatibility, and recovery.

## Try a small exercise

Why inspect an EF Core migration after renaming a property?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The generated change might look like dropping one column and adding another rather than preserving the existing data through a rename. Review and adjust the intended schema operation before applying it.

cards.front: What does an N+1 query problem look like in an EF Core web page?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The page loads a list with one query, then triggers another query for each item's related data. As the list grows, database round trips grow too. A deliberate projection, suitable eager loading, or another measured query design can fetch the needed data more efficiently.

## A worked example

An order list loads 50 orders, then separately retrieves each customer name. That can mean 51 queries. Project the needed order and customer fields in an appropriate query, and inspect the resulting SQL and number of round trips.

## Picture it another way

Walking back to the store for one ingredient at a time is slower than planning a suitable shopping trip.

## A common mistake

Loading every relationship eagerly can create a different performance problem, such as duplicated rows and very large result sets. Fetch what the screen actually needs and measure.

## Try a small exercise

Why might enabling lazy loading hide a performance issue until the list gets large?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Each property access can trigger additional database work. Small examples hide the accumulated round-trip cost; inspect query counts under realistic list sizes.

cards.front: What transaction guarantee does one EF Core SaveChanges call normally provide with a supporting provider?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The changes in that call are normally saved in a transaction so they succeed together or roll back together. A workflow spanning several saves may need an explicit transaction. A database transaction does not automatically include external email or HTTP effects.

## A worked example

Updating an order and its local audit row in one SaveChanges can keep those database changes together. Sending an email afterward is a separate effect. Use a durable workflow or outbox when the database change and eventual notification need reliable coordination.

## Picture it another way

A clerk can submit a bundle of forms to one records office atomically. That does not automatically control a separate courier company delivering a message.

## A common mistake

A transaction alone does not eliminate every race in a read-then-write rule. Isolation, constraints, conditional updates, and retry design may still matter.

## Try a small exercise

If an email was sent and the later database transaction rolls back, is the email automatically unsent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** The external effect is outside the database transaction. Design the ordering, durable intent, idempotency, and recovery behavior explicitly.

cards.front: How can an EF Core concurrency token help prevent silently overwriting another edit?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The update checks that the stored version still matches the version originally read. If another writer changed it, the save can report a concurrency conflict. The application then decides whether to reject, reload, merge, or retry according to the feature's rules.

## A worked example

Two users open version 4 of a note. One saves version 5. The second update includes the original version 4 and detects that it is stale. A provider-specific rowversion or an application-managed token can implement this pattern.

## Picture it another way

A document checkout slip records the edition you edited. The clerk notices if a newer edition was filed before accepting your changes.

## A common mistake

Do not silently retry every stale edit by overwriting the new data. That can erase the very change the concurrency check was meant to protect.

## Try a small exercise

Is SQL Server rowversion a portable wall-clock timestamp you can assume every EF Core provider supports?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It is a provider-specific version mechanism, not a general date/time value. Choose a concurrency token strategy appropriate to the actual database provider.

cards.front: Do validation attributes on a Minimal API DTO always run automatically without configuration?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

No. The application needs an appropriate validation mechanism. .NET 10 provides Minimal API validation support that is enabled through AddValidation with the required package setup. Controllers with ApiController follow their own model-validation behavior. Neither mechanism replaces domain or authorization checks.

## A worked example

For a .NET 10 Minimal API using Microsoft.Extensions.Validation, register AddValidation before Build and put supported validation attributes on the input type. Alternatively, perform deliberate explicit checks and return a consistent validation response. Follow the project's chosen mechanism.

## Picture it another way

Writing rules on a form does not guarantee anyone checks them. The processing desk must actually run the checks before accepting the form.

Do not copy controller-specific assumptions into Minimal APIs or claim that a type annotation alone rejects blank input. Verify behavior with an invalid HTTP request.

cards.front: How are authentication and authorization different in ASP.NET Core?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Authentication establishes an identity from a configured mechanism such as a session cookie or a validated token. Authorization checks whether that identity may perform an action. Knowing a user's name does not establish permission to read every note or administer the app.

## A worked example

A request may contain a valid user identity yet fail a policy requiring an administrator role. Another request may pass a general signed-in policy but still lack access to the specific note ID being requested.

## Picture it another way

Showing a library card identifies a member. It does not make that member a librarian with permission to change everyone's account.

## A common mistake

Do not trust a user ID in a request body as authenticated identity. The server derives trusted identity from its configured, verified authentication process.

## Try a small exercise

If a browser sends `{ "userId": "admin" }`, has it authenticated as an administrator?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** That is untrusted input. Authentication must validate the configured credential or session, and authorization must enforce the relevant permissions.

Register a CanExport policy using the app's trusted identity model, then require it on export endpoints. For a record-specific operation, also check access to that resource; a broad export capability need not grant access to every tenant's data.

Do not treat a claim sent by the browser as trusted just because it has a useful name. Claims are meaningful only within a correctly verified identity and issuance policy.

<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A valid signed-in user can still request someone else's ID. Scope the database lookup or perform a resource authorization check using verified identity. Apply the same rule to reads, updates, deletes, downloads, and background operations that act on private records.

## A worked example

A personal-note lookup filters by both the requested Id and the authenticated OwnerId. Shared notes need explicit membership rules. A hidden frontend button or a random-looking key is not an access check.

## Picture it another way

A hotel guest can know another room number without being allowed to open its door. The requested number and permission are separate facts.

## A common mistake

Do not accept OwnerId from the request as proof that the caller owns the record. Derive or validate the authority on the server.

## Try a small exercise

A user changes /notes/7 to /notes/8 manually. Which server check should prevent leaking another user's note?

<!-- recall:solution -->

An ownership or resource-authorization check tied to the verified caller. Route parsing and successful sign-in alone do not prove access to note 8.

cards.front: Why use a maintained identity system instead of inventing password and session handling for a .NET web app?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Identity features involve password verification, recovery, session behavior, lockout, and many edge cases. ASP.NET Core Identity or an appropriate external identity provider can supply established components. You still need correct integration, secure configuration, and application-specific authorization.

## A worked example

A web app can use a supported identity flow to establish its user and then apply note ownership policies. It should not store plaintext passwords or implement a home-grown token signature format merely to simplify a tutorial.

## Picture it another way

Use a tested lock mechanism and install it correctly. Buying a reliable lock does not automatically decide who should receive which key.

## A common mistake

Choosing an identity library does not make every endpoint private. Registration, login, recovery, and protected routes all need deliberate behavior and verification.

## Try a small exercise

Does using ASP.NET Core Identity remove the need to check which records a signed-in user may access?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It supplies identity-related capabilities. Your application must still enforce resource and action permissions for its own data.

cards.front: Why do cookie-authenticated .NET forms need the appropriate antiforgery protection?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A browser may attach its cookies to qualifying requests automatically. An attacker can try to induce an unwanted mutation through that browser. Antiforgery mechanisms help verify the intended request context; the required setup depends on whether you use MVC, Razor Pages, Minimal APIs, and particular input types.

## A worked example

Use the framework's supported antiforgery flow for cookie-authenticated forms and validate the token where required. Keep mutation actions out of GET endpoints. Token-in-header APIs have a different credential model that must be assessed on its own terms.

## Picture it another way

A familiar courier badge does not prove you approved every form the courier carries. The instruction needs an appropriate authenticity check too.

## A common mistake

Do not assume CORS is a complete antiforgery defense or that every Minimal API request automatically has identical form protections. Verify the actual configured endpoint behavior.

## Try a small exercise

If a request includes a valid session cookie, does that alone prove the user intentionally submitted a change?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Cookies can accompany induced browser requests. Apply the appropriate antiforgery and origin-related defenses for the application's credential and form model.

cards.front: Why is Razor's normal text encoding useful when displaying a user-supplied note?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Ordinary Razor rendering encodes text for its HTML context so markup-like characters are displayed as data. Bypassing that behavior can cause untrusted content to be interpreted as HTML. If rich content is required, use an appropriate sanitization policy rather than trusting raw input.

## A worked example

In a Razor view, normal rendering such as `@Model.Title` treats a title as text. Using Html.Raw on arbitrary user content intentionally bypasses that encoding. In Blazor, MarkupString likewise deserves deliberate treatment because it represents markup.

## Picture it another way

A printed quotation should remain quoted words, not become instructions for operating the printing press.

## A common mistake

Encoding for HTML text is not a universal solution for SQL, URLs, JavaScript contexts, or arbitrary HTML attributes. Use the safe API suited to each destination.

## Try a small exercise

Should a developer use Html.Raw merely to display a plain-text user comment containing angle brackets?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Normal encoded output is appropriate for plain text. Only introduce interpreted markup when the feature intentionally supports it and applies suitable safety rules.

name: 09 · Choose and build a .NET web UI
description: Choose between MVC, Razor Pages, and Blazor, then reason about forms, rendering, and state.

cards.front: How do MVC, Razor Pages, and Blazor offer different ways to build a .NET web interface?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

MVC organizes request handling around controllers and views. Razor Pages organizes server-rendered features around pages and page models. Blazor organizes UI with Razor components and selectable rendering approaches. Choose according to interaction needs, hosting, and team familiarity rather than assuming every app needs a separate JavaScript frontend.

## A worked example

A mostly form-based admin site can fit Razor Pages. An existing controller-oriented site may fit MVC. A component-rich interactive app may fit Blazor. A React frontend calling an ASP.NET Core API is another valid architecture with its own client/server boundary.

## Picture it another way

Several floor plans can serve the same shop. Choose the layout that fits how people actually move through the building.

## A common mistake

Do not confuse Razor syntax with a single rendering model. Razor appears in both server-rendered views/pages and Blazor components, with different lifecycles and capabilities.

## Try a small exercise

Does choosing ASP.NET Core require the browser UI to be written in React?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** ASP.NET Core can support server-rendered MVC or Razor Pages, Blazor, or an API used by a separate frontend. The UI architecture is a deliberate choice.

cards.front: What are the main roles of a controller and a view in ASP.NET Core MVC?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A controller action handles a request, coordinates application work, and chooses a result. A view renders HTML using an appropriate model. Keep important business and persistence rules in suitable services rather than hiding all of them inside markup.

## A worked example

A Notes controller action retrieves authorized note summaries and passes a view model to a Razor view. The view loops over summaries to render links. The controller should not hand the view a database context and expect rendering to decide the access policy.

## Picture it another way

A coordinator gathers the right information; a presenter lays it out for the audience. Those responsibilities cooperate without being identical.

## A common mistake

An API controller returning JSON and an MVC controller returning a view have different response purposes. Naming something Controller alone does not determine the client contract.

## Try a small exercise

Should a Razor view independently decide which private database records the caller is allowed to read?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The authorization and retrieval should happen through the appropriate server-side application boundary before rendering. A view should receive data the user is allowed to see.

cards.front: How do OnGet and OnPost handlers fit a Razor Pages feature?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The page model can use OnGet to prepare a page and OnPost to process a submitted form. Async variants support awaited work. Bound properties carry input, and the handler checks validity and permissions before making changes.

## A worked example

A Create Note page displays its form on GET. On POST, it validates the bound request, creates a note for the verified user, awaits the save, and redirects after success. Invalid input returns the page with useful validation messages.

## Picture it another way

A service form has a display step and a submission step. Showing the form should not itself create a record.

## A common mistake

Do not mutate important state merely because OnGet ran. Links, refreshes, and automated retrieval should not unexpectedly submit a form action.

## Try a small exercise

Why should a Razor Pages OnPost handler check ModelState.IsValid before persisting ordinary form input?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It confirms that the applicable binding and validation checks passed. The handler still needs authorization and domain checks before accepting the change.

cards.front: How does the post-redirect-get pattern help a successful server-rendered form?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

After processing the POST, the server redirects the browser to a GET page. Refreshing that destination then retrieves the page instead of resubmitting the same POST in the usual flow. This improves navigation, but does not provide complete duplicate-action protection by itself.

## A worked example

A note form saves successfully and redirects to its detail page. The address bar now points to the readable note URL. Invalid input can return the form directly with errors because there was no successful creation to redirect from.

## Picture it another way

After handing in an order, the clerk sends you to the receipt desk. Looking at the receipt again should not place the order again.

## A common mistake

A user can still submit twice, retry after a timeout, or use multiple tabs. Important mutation workflows may need idempotency or uniqueness protections in addition to this navigation pattern.

## Try a small exercise

Does post-redirect-get guarantee that two rapid POST requests cannot create duplicate records?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It changes the browser's normal post-success navigation. Server-side duplicate handling and concurrent request rules remain separate requirements.

cards.front: What does a Blazor component combine in one reusable unit?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A component describes a piece of markup and the C# state or behavior associated with it. Components can receive parameters and notify parents through callbacks. Their interactive behavior depends on the rendering mode and hosting configuration.

## A worked example

A NoteCard component can receive a title parameter and display it. The parent owns the list of notes. If a card exposes a delete action, it can notify the parent instead of secretly managing a second independent copy of the whole list.

## Picture it another way

A dashboard instrument receives readings and reports user actions, while the control system coordinates the larger machine.

## A common mistake

Do not assume every Razor component is interactive merely because its file contains an event handler. Static server rendering alone does not activate browser interaction.

## Try a small exercise

If a Blazor button renders but its C# click handler never runs, what configuration should you inspect?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Check whether the component has an appropriate interactive render mode and supporting app setup. Visible HTML from static rendering alone does not establish an active interactive component.

cards.front: How do Interactive Server and Interactive WebAssembly differ in a Blazor Web App?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Interactive Server runs component logic on the server and communicates with the browser over a live connection. Interactive WebAssembly runs client component logic in the browser after downloading the needed assets. Static server rendering supplies HTML without that interactive runtime behavior.

## A worked example

A server-interactive screen depends on connectivity to its circuit. A WebAssembly client may continue certain local interactions, but protected data operations still need server authorization and network access as designed. Neither mode automatically grants the whole app reliable offline behavior.

## Picture it another way

One remote control sends each action to a central operator; another device can perform some actions locally. Their connection and download needs differ.

## A common mistake

Do not ship server secrets into WebAssembly assets. Code and configuration delivered to the browser can be inspected by the person running it.

## Try a small exercise

Can a Blazor WebAssembly client safely contain a private database connection string because its source language is C#?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Client-delivered code and settings are inspectable. Keep private credentials and authoritative data access on an appropriate server boundary.

cards.front: Why should a Blazor child component usually notify its parent when parent-owned data needs to change?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The parent is the authoritative owner of that state. Parameters pass data downward, while callbacks communicate intended changes upward. This avoids confusing competing copies and keeps rerendering behavior easier to understand.

## A worked example

A note editor receives a title and an EventCallback for saving. It can keep a deliberate local draft, then notify the parent on save. The parent updates the list after the actual save succeeds or handles the failure explicitly.

## Picture it another way

A branch office proposes an update to the central register instead of editing an unofficial duplicate and assuming every other office saw it.

## A common mistake

Blindly mutating a parameter inside a child can be overwritten by the parent's next render. Distinguish local draft state from the committed parent value.

## Try a small exercise

If a child edits a private draft, should the parent assume it was durably saved merely because the textbox changed?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** A draft and a saved result are different states. Use an explicit save interaction and communicate the confirmed result or error through the intended contract.

name: 10 · Test and debug .NET web apps
description: Write tests that check real behavior and trace a broken request from the browser to storage.

cards.front: What should a small C# unit test establish about a business rule?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It should set up a meaningful input, run the rule, and check an independently reasoned result. Focus on behavior rather than private helper calls. Boundary and invalid-input cases often reveal more than many nearly identical happy-path examples.

## A worked example

For a title rule allowing up to 100 characters, test 99, 100, and 101, plus blank input if that is forbidden. The expected outcomes come from the requirement, not from calling the implementation again inside the assertion.

## Picture it another way

A measuring jig checks whether a part fits a known requirement. Measuring it with the same faulty ruler used to cut it can hide the mistake.

## A common mistake

A unit test that bypasses HTTP does not establish route binding, middleware, authentication, or database-provider behavior. Use the right test level for those boundaries.

## Try a small exercise

If a pure title-validation unit test passes, has it proven that ASP.NET Core invokes that validation during a real POST?

cards.front: Why can EF Core's InMemory provider miss defects in a relational production query?

<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It does not behave like the production relational database in important areas such as SQL translation and relational constraints. A fast fake can be useful for some tests, but query and persistence guarantees need a suitable real-provider test strategy.

Practicing on a painted cardboard lock does not establish that a real metal lock will turn the same way.

cards.front: What are three useful limits for a .NET API that lists a growing table?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Limit the number of rows, project only necessary fields, and use an appropriate indexed filtering and ordering strategy. These choices reduce transfer, memory, and database work. Validate client-provided limits and measure the actual query plan under representative data.

## A worked example

A note list returns 20 summaries containing ID, title, and update time. Full note bodies are retrieved only when needed. A stable cursor identifies the next page; a suitable index supports the access-scoped ordering.

## Picture it another way

A catalog page lists short descriptions, not every warehouse item and its full manual. Fetch detail when the reader asks for it.

ToListAsync is still capable of loading an enormous result. Async avoids blocking the wait; it does not automatically limit data volume or memory consumption.

## Try a small exercise

Does switching ToList to ToListAsync fix an endpoint that loads a million unnecessary rows?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It changes waiting behavior, not the amount of requested data. Add appropriate filtering, projection, paging, and limits.

cards.front: Why must a cache key for private .NET API data account for the caller's access scope?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A cached response may be reused without rerunning the original computation. If the key ignores ownership or tenant boundaries, one caller can receive another's data. Some responses should not be cached at all; others require explicit scope and invalidation rules.

Caching a private note list under a global key named notes can mix users. A deliberate design considers the verified user or tenant, filters, permissions, and freshness. HTTP output caching and an application object cache also have different rules.

Do not assume IMemoryCache is shared across all server instances. Each process has its own memory cache, which affects consistency and invalidation.

## Plain English
