A temporary read failure may allow a small number of retries within a deadline. A create-order request needs appropriate idempotency because the first attempt may have succeeded before its response was lost. Do not automatically retry a deterministic validation error.

## Picture it another way

Repeating a question can help if the line dropped. Repeating an order can create two deliveries if the first order already reached the shop.

## A common mistake

Independent retry loops at several service layers can multiply the number of attempts. Account for the whole request chain and honor cancellation.

## Try a small exercise

A payment request times out after the server may have processed it. Is a blind repeat automatically safe?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Use the provider's idempotency and outcome-reconciliation contract. A timeout does not prove that the first attempt had no effect.

cards.back:

## Plain English

Liveness asks whether the process should be considered alive or restarted. Readiness asks whether it should receive traffic now. Startup, required initialization, and dependency conditions can make those answers differ. Design checks around the hosting platform's actual actions.

## A worked example

A service may be running while it warms required data. Readiness can stay false until that work finishes. A brief shared database outage should not automatically cause every instance to restart unless that is the intended, justified recovery behavior.

## Picture it another way

A restaurant can have staff inside while the kitchen is not ready to accept orders. Turning the lights on and opening for service are different milestones.

## A common mistake

A health endpoint that always returns OK cannot establish that every important dependency or feature works. Define what it checks and keep expensive checks bounded.

Does a 200 response from a basic liveness endpoint prove that an authenticated note save works?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** It establishes only the liveness conditions implemented there. Readiness, integration checks, and operation-level monitoring cover other aspects of service behavior.

cards.back:

## Plain English

Publishing creates deployable output for the selected target and settings. Framework-dependent output expects a compatible runtime on the host. Self-contained output includes the needed runtime for its target, but the application owner must still rebuild and deploy runtime updates.

## A worked example

For a real project directory, `dotnet publish -c Release` creates release publish output using that project's configuration. Deployment then supplies environment settings, a host, and any required runtime according to the chosen publish mode.

## Picture it another way

A recipe is source code; a packaged meal ready for delivery is publish output. The packaging still needs to match its destination.

## A common mistake

Do not assume self-contained means maintenance-free or cross-platform for every output. Runtime identifier, architecture, native dependencies, and patching still matter.

## Try a small exercise

If you deploy framework-dependent .NET output, what must the server normally provide?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A compatible installed runtime, along with the application's required configuration and hosting environment. The SDK used to build the app is not usually required merely to run published output.

cards.front: What should a .NET background worker consider when the host is shutting down?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Observe the shutdown signal, stop accepting new work as appropriate, and complete or safely release in-progress work within the allowed time. Important jobs need recovery if the process ends before completion. A graceful-stop opportunity is useful but not guaranteed for every failure.

## A worked example

A queue worker receives cancellation while processing a job. It can stop fetching more jobs, finish a safe current step, and acknowledge only according to the queue's completion rules. A later worker may need to retry unfinished work without duplicating effects.

## Picture it another way

At closing time, stop taking new orders and account for each unfinished ticket. A fire alarm may still force an earlier exit.

## A common mistake

Do not rely on a finally block as the only durability strategy. Abrupt termination, machine failure, and forced shutdown can prevent cleanup from completing.

## Try a small exercise

Does a graceful-shutdown handler guarantee that every queued job survives a power failure?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Durable storage and recoverable processing handle abrupt failure. Graceful shutdown only helps when the process receives time to cooperate.

cards.front: How can logs, metrics, and traces complement each other in a .NET service?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Metrics show aggregate trends such as error rates and latency. Logs record specific events and context. Traces connect work across operations and services. Correlation lets you move from a detected problem to an example request and its relevant path.

## A worked example

A rising error-rate metric points to failed note saves. A trace shows most time in a dependency call, and correlated logs identify a safe failure category. Record useful identifiers while avoiding secret or unnecessary personal payloads.

## Picture it another way

A dashboard shows traffic congestion, a route map shows the affected journey, and an incident note explains one blockage.

## A common mistake

Averages can hide slow experiences for some users. Use appropriate distributions and avoid unbounded metric labels such as unique request IDs that create excessive cardinality.

## Try a small exercise

Why is a unique request ID often useful in logs but a poor label for an aggregate metric?

<!-- recall:solution -->

It helps correlate a particular event, but each unique metric label creates another time series. High-cardinality labels can make metrics expensive and hard to use.

cards.front: What would a small vertical slice of a .NET notes app include?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It connects one useful behavior across the necessary layers: request input, validation, authorization, business work, persistence, and response. Start with a small complete path rather than building many disconnected abstractions whose cooperation has not been tested.

A first slice can create a note for a verified user and return its public ID and title. Verify invalid input, allowed creation, and persistence. Later slices can add listing, editing, and search while reusing only the boundaries that prove useful.

Build one working room with power, plumbing, and a door before duplicating a design across an entire building.

A vertical slice does not mean ignoring separation of responsibilities. Keep the feature understandable without introducing layers that have no clear current purpose.

It proves how real input moves through the system and reveals the actual boundaries needed. Empty abstractions alone cannot demonstrate a usable feature or a correct data flow.

cards.front: What sequence should a .NET create-note endpoint establish before returning a created response?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Bind the allowed request, validate its content, establish the caller's rights, construct the entity with server-owned fields, and await persistence. Then return an appropriate public response and location. Each step establishes something the next step relies on.

## A worked example

The client supplies a title and body. The server supplies OwnerId and CreatedAt. After SaveChangesAsync succeeds, the response includes the generated ID. A storage failure takes a failure path rather than returning a fabricated saved record.

## Picture it another way

An official receipt is issued after the records office accepts a valid form, not while the form is still being checked.

## A common mistake

Do not allow the client to submit arbitrary internal entity fields or return a database object containing information outside the public API contract.

## Try a small exercise

Should a create-note response claim a saved ID before the awaited persistence step completes successfully?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Report completed creation only after its required save succeeds. If the design merely accepts a background job, use a distinct documented job-status contract.

cards.front: What should a .NET notes-list endpoint return for a small phone screen?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Return a bounded, access-scoped page of summaries with the fields needed to recognize and open each note. Include stable ordering and a way to request more. Large bodies and unrelated fields belong in an appropriate detail request when the screen does not need them yet.

## A worked example

A page contains note ID, title, and last-updated time, with at most 20 results. The query filters by the verified owner before projection and paging. The UI distinguishes loading, empty results, and an error instead of showing the same blank panel.

## Picture it another way

A table of contents helps you pick a chapter without downloading and displaying every chapter on the first screen.

## A common mistake

Do not page all tenants together and filter the returned objects in the browser. Access scope belongs in the authoritative server query or equivalent permission boundary.

## Try a small exercise

Why must an owner filter happen before returning a notes-list response, even if the frontend hides other users' entries?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Returning the data already exposes it to the client. The server must avoid supplying records outside the caller's permission scope in the first place.

cards.front: What should a .NET note-edit flow do when the stored note changed after the user opened it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Detect the stale version when the feature requires conflict protection, then give a defined outcome such as a conflict response and a reload or merge path. Preserve the user's draft where practical. Silently overwriting the newer data can lose another person's work.

## A worked example

The edit request contains the allowed fields and the version the user read. The server checks access and applies a version-aware save. A conflict returns useful safe context so the UI can retain the draft while asking the user to reconcile changes.

## Picture it another way

Two editors submit changes to the same manuscript edition. The publisher needs to notice that the edition changed rather than blindly replacing the latest draft.

## A common mistake

A disabled Save button only reduces duplicate clicks in one page. It does not coordinate other tabs, other users, or another server instance.

## Try a small exercise

Why keep the unsaved draft visible after an edit conflict instead of clearing the form?

<!-- recall:solution -->

The draft may contain valuable work the user needs to compare or reapply. A conflict means the base version is stale, not that the user's intended changes should be discarded.

cards.front: What decisions belong in a .NET delete-note endpoint contract?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Define who may delete the record, whether deletion is permanent or logical, what happens to related data, and the response when the record is already absent. Clients may retry a request after losing its response, so repeated attempts need an understandable policy.

## A worked example

An authorized delete removes the intended note and returns no content. A repeat may return the same no-content result or a documented not-found outcome. A soft-delete design must ensure ordinary queries consistently exclude deleted records where appropriate.

## Picture it another way

Canceling a reservation needs a policy for both the first request and a caller asking again because they never received the confirmation.

## A common mistake

Soft deletion is not automatically privacy erasure or complete protection from accidental exposure. Retention, backups, access rules, and all query paths still need deliberate behavior.

## Try a small exercise

Does returning a different status for an already-deleted record necessarily mean DELETE cannot be idempotent?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No.** Idempotency concerns the intended server effect of repeating the operation, not identical response text or status in every case. Document the response policy for callers.

cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Specify which fields are searchable, how case and whitespace are handled, allowed query length, access scope, ordering, and result limits. Database collation and search capabilities affect behavior and performance. A simple C# string method does not automatically express every database search requirement.

## A worked example

A first search can trim the input, reject unreasonable length, and query only the caller's notes with a bounded result size. Test empty input and case behavior against the actual database provider. Add more advanced search only when its user requirement is clear.

## Picture it another way

A catalog search needs rules for spelling and categories before a clerk can reliably interpret every request.

## A common mistake

Do not load every private note into memory merely to apply an unrestricted contains search. Keep the access boundary and workload limits intact.

## Try a small exercise

Why test case-insensitive note search against the production database provider rather than only a C# list?

<!-- recall:solution -->

Database collation, translation, and matching rules can differ from in-memory string comparisons. The test should establish the behavior the real query will produce.

cards.front: What extra work does adding attachments introduce to a .NET notes app?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An upload needs size and type policy, controlled storage naming, access checks, and a defined relationship to its note. File storage and database metadata may fail independently, so design cleanup and recovery. Download routes must enforce access as carefully as the note routes.

## A worked example

An endpoint accepts a bounded permitted attachment, stores it under a generated identifier, and records metadata for the authorized note. If a later step fails, account for any orphaned file. A filename supplied by the client is display data, not an authoritative storage path.

## Picture it another way

Checking a parcel into a cloakroom creates both a physical item and a claim record. The system must keep them associated and handle an incomplete check-in.

## A common mistake

Do not trust an extension such as .jpg as proof of file contents or combine an untrusted filename directly with a server filesystem path.

## Try a small exercise

Why does a private attachment download need its own authorization check even if the upload endpoint was protected?

<!-- recall:solution -->

A different caller may later obtain or guess its URL. Access must be checked when serving the file, not only when accepting it into storage.
